msbuild-props.md:1389 "The `DisableTransitiveProjectReferences` property controls implicit project references. Set this property to `true` to disable implicit `ProjectReference` items. Disabling implicit project references results in non-transitive behavior". Supports the transitive part. No doc states the 'only when' exclusivity, and in general a <Reference> to a DLL, a PackageReference, or a ProjectReference from Directory.Build.props also works.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: In Đơn Hàng, a project's code can name another project's types because its .csproj lists that project in a ProjectReference, or references a project that does, so the ProjectReference lines show where arrows can start.

issues.text: New in round 2, in changed text. The sentence states a general .NET rule: 'only when its .csproj file references that project'. The docs support transitive ProjectReference (DisableTransitiveProjectReferences) but not the 'only': a <Reference> to the built DLL, a PackageReference, or a ProjectReference added from Directory.Build.props also lets code name the types. It holds in Đơn Hàng: grepping *.csproj/*.props finds only csproj ProjectReference items.
issues.quote: A project's code can name another project's types only when its `.csproj` file references that project, directly or through a project it references
